paper_topic: metabench: a sparse, IRT-based distillation of six Open-LLM-Leaderboard benchmarks (ARC, GSM8K, HellaSwag, MMLU, TruthfulQA, WinoGrande) to under 3% of their combined size

nodes.text: Large Language Models (LLMs) represent a significant leap forward in our quest to emulate human-like understanding and generation of language (Brown et al., 2020).
These sophisticated algorithms are designed to process, interpret, and produce language with unprecedented accuracy and fluency (Bubeck et al., 2023).

By training on vast datasets encompassing a myriad of linguistic patterns, LLMs have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in tasks ranging from simple text completion (Radford et al., 2019) to complex problem-solving (Chen et al., 2021a) and creative writing (Elkins & Chun, 2020).

Their potential to transform various fields—education (Kasneci et al., 2023), customer service (Pandya & Holia, 2023), content creation (Zhang et al., 2023), and beyond—has captured the imagination of researchers and practitioners alike (Bommasani et al., 2021; Bubeck et al., 2023).
However, as these models grow in complexity, so does the challenge of effectively evaluating their diverse abilities (Burnell et al., 2023; Ke et al., 2023).
Traditionally, research has relied on extensive benchmarks—vast arrays of tasks—to assess the abilities of LLMs (Srivastava et al., 2023; Raji et al., 2021).
However, these benchmarks often measure overlapping skills, leading to redundancy and inefficiency.

This paper introduces metabench, a sparse benchmark engineered to distill the essence of six prominent benchmarks—ARC (Clark et al., 2018), GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019), MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021), TruthfulQA (Lin et al., 2022), and WinoGrande (Sakaguchi et al., 2020)—into a more concise and informative benchmark.
By analyzing data from over 5000 LLMs, we identified the most revealing items within these benchmarks, compressing them to less than 3% of their combined size.
We also provide adaptive testing simulations that suggest that the number of items administered to LLMs can be lowered even further.
This volume reduction greatly enhances evaluation efficiency, while also maintaining the original benchmarks' ability to measure underlying abilities.
The metabench framework leverages psychometric techniques (Hambleton & Swaminathan, 2013; Wang et al., 2023a) to estimate the latent abilities captured by these benchmarks (Burnell et al., 2023).
nodes.display_label: Use psychometrics to estimate latent abilities

nodes.text: These estimates can reconstruct individual and total benchmark scores with minimal error, and reveal a single underlying factor that captures most of their variability.
By refining how we measure the abilities of LLMs, metabench offers a new lens through which we can understand and improve them.
nodes.display_label: New lens for LLM ability measurement

nodes.text: Practitioners can run their own models on this efficient and highly informative benchmark, obtain approximated scores, and compute an overall estimate of their models' general ability.
We additionally offer a second, disjoint version of metabench for users that intend to evaluate an LLM multiple times.
nodes.display_label: Disjoint second version for repeat eval

nodes.text: Our work underscores the potential for more streamlined and psychologically meaningful evaluation methods (Coda-Forno et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2023).
It is aimed for the open-source community and independent machine learning researchers with limited resources.

We use data from n > 5000 LLMs to identify the most informative items of six benchmarks, ARC, GSM8K, HellaSwag, MMLU, TruthfulQA and WinoGrande (with d = 28,632 items in total). From them we distill a sparse benchmark, metabench, that has less than 3% of the original size of all six benchmarks combined.
This new sparse benchmark goes beyond point scores by yielding estimators of the underlying benchmark-specific abilities.
We show that these estimators (1) can be used to reconstruct each original individual benchmark score with, on average, 1.24% root mean square error (RMSE),
(2) reconstruct the original total score with 0.58% RMSE, and
(3) have a single underlying common factor whose Spearman correlation with the total score is r = 0.94.

The intro itself opens with a five-sentence Context block (N1-N5) on LLM capability and the growing evaluation challenge — the para-1 'However' at N4->N5 introduces the paper-theme ('challenge of evaluating diverse abilities') and is correctly typed Context per the Para-1 'However' rule.

The Method block (N8-N18) is unusually long for a benchmark intro because the paper organizes its rationale-of-design into a contiguous prose block: introducing metabench (N8), the 5000-LLM compression to <3% (N9), adaptive-testing extension (N10), the psychometric framing (N12), score-reconstruction reveal (N13, typed Result since it's an empirical claim about the method's behavior), and a series of practitioner-oriented promises (N14-N18).
